items.title: Study methods that work
items.description: Retrieval, spacing and interleaving, and why rereading feels better than it works.

pages.title: Retrieval and spacing
pages.markdown:
# Retrieval and spacing

Testing yourself works better than rereading, because remembering is the skill you are training. Close the book and write what you recall; the effort of reconstruction is what consolidates the material.

Space the reviews instead of repeating them in one sitting. Forgetting a little between sessions is useful: the second retrieval is harder and therefore worth more.

**In practice** — three short self-tests across a week beat one long rereading session.

pages.title: Interleaving and feedback
pages.markdown:
# Interleaving and feedback

Practise related topics in mixed order. Blocked practice (ten of the same exercise) feels smoother, but mixed practice teaches you to choose the method, which is what an exam or a real problem asks for.

Seek feedback quickly. A correction applied while the attempt is still fresh changes the next attempt; the same correction a week later mostly changes nothing.

items.title: Note-taking that survives
items.description: Notes as a tool for thinking, not a transcript of the lesson.

pages.title: Notes as thinking
pages.markdown:
# Notes as thinking

A transcript copies; a note transforms. Write in your own words, leave space for a question, and mark what you did not understand — those marks are the most valuable part of the page.

One page, one idea. If a page needs three titles, it is three pages.

pages.title: Revisiting notes
pages.markdown:
# Revisiting notes

Notes that are never reopened are archives, not tools. A short pass a day later, then a week later, converts them into memory; a summary written from memory is better still.

Link notes to each other. A link you create is a connection you have already understood.

items.title: Asking better questions
items.description: Turning a vague difficulty into a question someone can answer.

pages.title: What makes a question answerable
pages.markdown:
# What makes a question answerable

A good question states what you tried, what you expected and what happened. That triad lets someone else reproduce the problem, and often makes the answer obvious to you before it arrives.

Ask one question at a time. A message with four questions gets one answer.

pages.title: Answering well
pages.markdown:
# Answering well

Answer the question that was asked, then add context if it changes the answer. Saying 'it depends' without saying what it depends on is not an answer.

When you do not know, say so and say how you would find out.

items.title: Reading a scientific paper
items.description: A reading order that finds the claim, the evidence and the limits.

pages.title: A reading order
pages.markdown:
# A reading order

Start with the abstract, then the last paragraph of the introduction, then the figures. If the claim survives that, read the methods: who was studied, how many, and compared with what.

The discussion is the authors' interpretation, not their result. Keep the two apart in your notes.

pages.title: Finding the limits
pages.markdown:
# Finding the limits

Every study has a population, a size and a duration. Ask how far the finding travels beyond them: a result in twenty students over two weeks is a hypothesis, not a rule.

Note what the authors did not measure — it is often the most interesting part of the paper.

items.title: Giving feedback people can use
items.description: Specific, timely and about the work rather than the person.

pages.title: Specific and timely
pages.markdown:
# Specific and timely

'This paragraph is unclear' is an opinion; 'I lost the thread at the third sentence, where the subject changes' is an observation the author can act on.

Give feedback while the work is still being made. A remark on a finished project is a verdict, not a help.

pages.title: Receiving feedback
pages.markdown:
# Receiving feedback

Ask for the kind of feedback you want: on structure, on clarity, on accuracy. A vague request produces a vague answer.

Thank the reader, then decide. Feedback is information, not an order.

items.title: Presenting without reading slides
items.description: One idea per slide, a spoken argument, and rehearsing the transitions.

pages.title: Structure
pages.markdown:
# Structure

Say what you will show, show it, say what it meant. Three parts, five minutes, and the audience can follow without notes.

One idea per slide. If a slide needs a paragraph of explanation, the paragraph belongs in your voice.

pages.title: Delivery
pages.markdown:
# Delivery

Rehearse the transitions, not the sentences. A memorised script breaks at the first interruption; a clear next step survives one.

Leave silence after an important point. It is the cheapest emphasis available.
